ai.literal: Feeling shame because of improper deeds is true modesty indeed; the other kind of shyness is that of beautiful-foreheaded virtuous women.
ai.translation: To shrink in shame from improper deeds is true modesty; all other kinds of shyness are merely the natural bashfulness of beautiful-foreheaded women.
ai.modern: தீய செயல்களைச் செய்ய அஞ்சி நாணமடைவதே உண்மையான நாணமாகும்; மற்றவை எல்லாம் அழகிய நெற்றியையுடைய பெண்களின் இயற்கை நாணமே ஆகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet distinguishes between moral shame and natural bashfulness. The author states that true, essential modesty (நாண்) is the shrinking back from committing improper or evil deeds. Any other form of shyness, such as the natural reserve or bashfulness shown by beautiful women (திருநுதல் நல்லவர்), is of a different, non-moral kind. For a virtuous life, it is the dread of doing wrong that constitutes genuine modesty.

ai.literal: Food, clothing, and the rest, to all living beings, are not different; the possession of a sense of shame is human beings' distinction.
ai.translation: Food, clothing, and other basic needs are common to all living creatures; it is the possession of a sense of shame that is the unique distinction of human beings.
ai.modern: உணவு, உடை மற்றும் பிற அடிப்படைத் தேவைகள் எல்லா உயிர்களுக்கும் பொதுவானவை; ஆனால், நாணம் (பழிக்கு அஞ்சும் தன்மை) கொண்டிருப்பதே மனிதர்களுக்குரிய சிறந்த தனித்தன்மையாகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights what truly defines humanity. While biological needs like food, clothing, and other basic necessities (referred to as 'eccam') are shared by all living creatures, they do not make humans unique. The poet uses the word 'nan' to mean a moral sensitivity or a healthy sense of shame that shrinks from doing wrong. It is this possession of a moral conscience ('nanutaimai') that serves as the true distinction ('cirappu') of human beings ('mantar') over other forms of life.

ai.literal: All lives that have flesh as their basis; nobility has as its basis the virtue called shame.
ai.translation: Just as all physical life depends on the flesh for its existence, perfect nobility depends on the virtue called a sense of shame.
ai.modern: உடலை அடிப்படையாகக் கொண்டுதான் எல்லா உயிர்களும் வாழ்கின்றன; அதுபோல, சால்பு என்னும் சான்றாண்மை நாணம் என்னும் நற்பண்பை அடிப்படையாகக் கொண்டது.
ai.explanation: This couplet draws a beautiful analogy between physical existence and moral character. Every living being in the world requires a physical body of flesh to exist. In the exact same way, a person's perfect character or nobility (sālpu) cannot exist without the foundational virtue of 'nāṇ' (a healthy sense of shame or dread of doing wrong). The poet emphasizes that just as a soul without a body cannot manifest, nobility without a sense of shame is impossible.

ai.literal: An ornament is it not, the possession of shame, to the noble? If that is not there, a disease is it not, their proud walk?
ai.translation: To the noble, possessing a sense of shame is indeed an ornament; if they lack it, their proud, majestic walk is nothing but a disease.
ai.modern: சான்றோர்க்கு நாணத்தைக் கொண்டிருப்பதுதான் சிறந்த அணிகலன் ஆகும்; அது இல்லாவிட்டால், அவர்கள் பெருமிதத்தோடு நடக்கும் நடையானது ஒரு நோயாகவே கருதப்படும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the importance of 'nāṇ' (a sense of shame or moral dread of doing wrong) for noble individuals. It states that having this sense of shame is the true ornament that beautifies their character. Without this inner quality, any outward display of dignity, such as a proud or majestic gait, is not a sign of greatness but rather a disease or a defect. The contrast between 'aṇi' (ornament) and 'piṇi' (disease) emphasizes that true dignity comes from moral sensitivity, not from mere external posture.

ai.literal: Those who feel shame for others' blame and their own blame, the world will call them the dwelling place for the virtue of shame.
ai.translation: The world will hail those who shrink in shame from both others' guilt and their own as the very abode of the virtue of modesty.
ai.modern: பிறருக்கு வரும் பழியையும் தமக்கு வரும் பழியையும் கண்டு நாணப்படுபவர்களை, இந்த உலகம் நாணம் என்னும் நற்பண்பின் உறைவிடம் என்று போற்றும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet defines the true depth of the virtue of shame. A highly ethical person does not merely feel shame for their own misdeeds; they are so sensitive to moral wrongs that they feel equally ashamed when others commit blameworthy acts. The world praises such individuals, recognizing them as the very home or dwelling place of the virtue of shame. Their capacity to feel others' guilt as their own represents the peak of moral empathy.

ai.literal: Without holding the sense of honor as their fence, indeed, the vast world, they will not desire, those who are noble.
ai.translation: Noble people will not desire even the vast world if they cannot have their sense of honor as its protective fence.
ai.modern: மேன்மையானவர்கள், நாணத்தை (தன்மானத்தை) ஒரு வேலியாகக் கொள்ளாமல், இந்த அகன்ற உலகத்தையே பெறுவதாக இருந்தாலும் அதனை விரும்ப மாட்டார்கள்.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the supreme value of 'nan' (the sense of shame or honor) for noble individuals. Great people would not desire to possess the entire vast world if they had to do so by compromising their self-respect. The metaphor of 'nan' as a 'veli' (fence) suggests that honor is what guards and defines a person's character. Without this boundary of self-respect, even the grandest worldly achievements are worthless to the noble.

ai.literal: For the sake of honor, life they will give up; for the sake of life, honor they will not give up, those who cherish honor.
ai.translation: Those who cherish a sense of honor will give up their life for the sake of honor; they will never give up their honor for the sake of life.
ai.modern: நாண உணர்வைப் போற்றி வாழ்பவர்கள், மானத்தைக் காப்பதற்காகத் தம் உயிரையும் விட்டுவிடுவார்கள்; ஆனால், உயிரைக் காப்பதற்காகத் தம் மானத்தை விட்டுவிட மாட்டார்கள்.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the supreme value of a sense of honor (nāṇ) over physical life itself. Those who truly cherish and practice honor will readily sacrifice their lives to preserve their integrity. Conversely, they will never compromise or abandon their honor just to save their own lives. The repetition of the words for honor (nāṇ) and life (uyir) emphasizes the stark choice between the two, showing that for noble minds, honor is far more precious than mere existence.

parts.gloss: he who does not feel ashamed

ai.literal: If oneself does not feel ashamed of that which is fit for others to feel ashamed, virtue possesses that which is fit to feel ashamed of him.
ai.translation: If a person does not feel ashamed of an act that makes onlookers feel ashamed, virtue itself will feel ashamed to remain with him.
ai.modern: பிறர் வெட்கப்படக்கூடிய ஒரு செயலுக்குத் தான் வெட்கப்படாமல் இருந்தால், அறமே அவனைக் கண்டு வெட்கப்பட்டு அவனை விட்டு நீங்கும் தன்மையைக் கொண்டிருக்கும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the critical role of a sense of shame in maintaining moral character. When a person commits a wrong deed that makes even others feel embarrassed on their behalf, yet remains shameless, they lose their moral compass. The poet personifies virtue (அறம்) to explain that it will feel ashamed to dwell with such a shameless person and will abandon them. Thus, shamelessness completely drives away all goodness and virtue.

ai.literal: Family lineage will burn if conduct is slipped; goodness will burn if shamelessness abides.
ai.translation: A slip in right conduct will destroy one's lineage; but if shamelessness takes root, it will destroy every good quality one possesses.
ai.modern: ஒருவர் தன் ஒழுக்கத்திலிருந்து தவறினால் அது அவருடைய குலத்தை அழிக்கும்; ஆனால் அவரிடம் வெட்கமின்மை நிலைத்து நின்றால், அது அவருடைய எல்லா நன்மைகளையும் அழித்துவிடும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet contrasts the consequences of failing in one's conduct with the far more devastating consequences of losing one's sense of shame. If a person slips from their principles of conduct, that failure destroys the reputation of their lineage. However, if shamelessness becomes a permanent state in them, it burns away and destroys all their inherent goodness and virtues. The poet uses the metaphor of burning to show how both failures act like a destructive fire, but shamelessness is the ultimate destroyer of a person's entire character.

ai.literal: The movement of those who do not have a sense of shame inside is like a wooden puppet simulating life by a string.
ai.translation: The movements of those who have no sense of shame in their hearts are like a wooden puppet merely mimicking life by the pulling of a string.
ai.modern: நெஞ்சில் நாண உணர்வு இல்லாதவர்களுடைய இயக்கம், மரப்பாவையை நூலினால் ஆட்டி உயிர் உள்ளதைப் போலக் காட்டி இயக்குவதைப் போன்றதாகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet employs a brilliant play on the word 'நாண்'. In the first line, 'நாண்' refers to the moral sense of shame or conscience. In the second line, 'நாணால்' refers to the string or cord used to manipulate a puppet. The poet explains that a person who lacks an inner sense of shame has no true human agency or dignity. Their actions and movements are entirely mechanical, resembling a lifeless wooden puppet that is made to simulate life only because someone else is pulling its strings.
